input.content:
---
type: architecture
title: "Architecture Overview"
description: "The celld workspace: three crates with a strict dependency direction — a pure decision core (celld-logic), the daemon/executor host (celld), and a vendored SQLite-to-object-store replication engine (celld-ltx) — plus the build profiles and pinned dependencies that shape the design."
tags: [architecture, workspace, crates, dependencies, build-profiles]
---

## What celld is

celld is a self-hosted daemon that runs Cloudflare Workers and Durable
Objects code on your own machines. Each object is a **cell** — a named
server with its own private SQLite database. A **node** is one `celld`
process, and the nodes that share one object-storage bucket form a
**fleet**: ownership of a cell is decided by a conditional bucket write,
there is no consensus service, and committed SQLite writes are replicated
as LTX data so acknowledged data survives node loss (RPO=0)
(`README.md:3-34`).

## The three-crate split

The workspace manifest opens by stating the rule the layout enforces:
*"Clean-sheet celld workspace. `crates/logic` owns all behavioral state and
decisions; `crates/celld` is only an effect executor and adapter host"*
(`Cargo.toml:1-5`). Dependency direction is strictly one way:

```
celld (daemon: V8 host, HTTP, CLI, effects)
 ├─→ celld-logic  (pure sans-IO decision core; zero dependencies)
 └─→ celld-ltx    (vendored SQLite WAL → object-store replication)
```

- **`celld-logic`** is the behavioral brain: `State`, `Event`, `Effect`,
  `on_event` as the only state transition, plus one module per policy
  (routing, gates, pressure, restore, wake, queue, alarm, cron, kv,
  isolate, log tier). See `openwiki/architecture/logic-decision-core.md`.
- **`celld`** is a library plus one binary (`[lib] path = "lib.rs"`,
  `[[bin]] name = "celld" path = "main.rs"`). It embeds V8 (`v8 = "152.1"`),
  runs the serial Actor that is the sole caller of `on_event`, and provides
  the listeners, CLI subcommands (`deploy`, `dev`, `diagnose`, `cell`,
  `d1`, `kv`, `queue`, …), object-store adapters, telemetry, and the JS API
  (`crates/celld/Cargo.toml:11-15`). The boundary mechanics are covered in
  `openwiki/architecture/execution-boundary.md`.
- **`celld-ltx`** is an embedded replication engine: *"in-process
  SQLite→object-store replication for celld"*, vendored on 2026-08-03 from
  rustyriver — itself a Rust reimplementation of Litestream v0.5 and the
  LTX format — and *"celld owns and evolves this snapshot; it does not
  track an upstream branch"*. It exists to serve celld's RPO=0 durability
  goal for every cell write (`crates/ltx/Cargo.toml:1-8`).

Notably, `celld-ltx` does **not** depend on `celld-logic`: replication is
mechanical storage work, and the durability *policy* stays in the core. The
LTX and logic crates are joined in `celld` by `ltx_repl.rs` (the in-process
backend) and executed under decisions from `celld_logic::log_tier` etc.
(`crates/celld/ltx_repl.rs:3-9`).

## Ownership of the big subsystems

`crates/celld` is a flat module list; the meaningful grouping is by job:

| Subsystem | Modules | Detail page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Execution domain | `actor.rs`, `asyncrt.rs`, `host_services.rs` | execution-boundary.md |
| Decisions | (all of `celld-logic`) | logic-decision-core.md |
| V8 runtime & JS APIs | `runtime.rs`, `js.rs` + `js/`, `pool.rs`, `storage.rs` | js-runtime-and-apis.md |
| Durability path | `ltx_repl.rs`, `replication.rs`, `node_log.rs` | durability-and-replication.md |
| Fleet coordination | `fleet.rs`, `ownership_store.rs`, `drain_token.rs`, `dead_node_gc.rs`, `wake.rs` | cells-and-ownership.md |
| Networking | `main.rs` (listeners), `main/peer_tunnel.rs`, `main/websocket.rs`, `peer_auth.rs`, `ws_client.rs`, `protocol.rs` | http-routing-and-peer-tunnel.md |
| Application lifecycle | `deploy.rs`, `generation.rs`, `assets.rs`, `dev.rs`, `local_store.rs` | deployments-and-dev.md |
| Object storage | `bucket.rs` (+ ltx `client/`) | object-storage.md |
| Cell-backed services | reserved classes via `logic::queue/kv/cron/alarm/wake`, `operator_cell.rs` | cell-services.md |
| Operations | `machine.rs`, `memory.rs`, `cli_options.rs`, `env_vars.rs`, `startup.rs`, `cell_cli.rs`, `d1_cli.rs`, `kv_cli.rs`, `queue_cli.rs`, `peer_probe.rs`, `control_plane.rs` | fleet-operations.md |
| Observability | `telemetry.rs`, `otlp.rs` | observability-and-telemetry.md |

`main.rs` states the binary/library split: *"The binary contains
connection, startup, shutdown, and V8 shell code. The library Actor owns
the execution domain and its routed adapters"* (`crates/celld/main.rs:2-4`).

## Build-shape decisions

- **Every direct dependency is declared once** in `[workspace.dependencies]`
  "so the crates can never drift onto two versions of the same crate;
  members add their own features" (`Cargo.toml:33-35`). `rusqlite` alignment
  is a hard constraint: `libsqlite3-sys` carries `links="sqlite3"`, so the
  workspace physically cannot hold two versions
  (`crates/ltx/Cargo.toml:36-38`).
- **Release is size-tuned**: fat LTO, `codegen-units = 1`, `opt-level =
  "s"` (not `"z"` — measure RPS before trading further), `panic = "abort"`
  to drop unwind tables, `strip = true` (`Cargo.toml:7-14`).
- **A second profile, `lab`**, is the fast experiment loop: release
  optimization minus the fat-LTO relink (`lto = "thin"`,
  `codegen-units = 16`, incremental) and *unstripped with line tables* so
  `perf` on a node attributes CPU by function; shipped artifacts stay on
  `release` (`Cargo.toml:16-27`).
- **Pins encode architectural decisions.** `fastwebsockets` is pinned to
  `=0.8.1` for the unstable `unstable-split` feature, because a WebSocket
  read is not cancel-safe and the tunnel needs independent read/write
  halves; the comment records that celld carries that risk knowingly
  (`Cargo.toml:50-59`). `sqlite-vec` is pinned `=0.1.9` to the audited C
  amalgamation (pre-v1 binding outside compatibility policy)
  (`Cargo.toml:116-118`). `v8 = "152.1"` is the first rusty_v8 carrying
  `v8::Locker` and `Send` `Globals`, which shared isolates need — the
  comment records the upstream issues (`Cargo.toml:136-140`).
- jemalloc with stats is the allocator, because the pressure classifier
  needs `stats.allocated` vs `stats.resident` — the pages the allocator
  keeps but no cell uses (`Cargo.toml:122-127`).

## Where to go next

- Reading order for behavior changes: `logic-decision-core.md` →
  `execution-boundary.md` → the relevant concept page.
- Operating the result: `openwiki/operations/fleet-operations.md`.
- How correctness is argued: `openwiki/testing/testing-strategy.md`.

Dependency direction is one-way: celld depends on celld-logic and celld-ltx; celld-ltx depends on tokio/rusqlite/object_store but on neither celld crate; celld-logic has zero dependencies.

celld-ltx is a snapshot vendored 2026-08-03 from rustyriver (a Rust reimplementation of Litestream v0.5 and the LTX format); celld owns and evolves the snapshot and does not track an upstream branch, and it exists to serve celld's RPO=0 durability goal for every cell write.

input.content:
---
type: change-guide
title: "Common Change Guides"
description: "Focused recipes for representative celld maintenance tasks: adding a core policy decision and its executor effect, adding a CELLD_* environment variable, extending the JS API surface, evolving bucket-resident protocol objects, bumping the peer protocol, and touching the storage dialect."
tags: [change-guide, maintenance, testing, env-vars, protocol]
---

Each guide names the owning seam and the narrowest validation that proves the
change. The governing rule everywhere: decisions go to `celld-logic`, effects
go to `celld` adapters, and nothing in between is allowed to drift (see
`openwiki/architecture/logic-decision-core.md` and
`openwiki/architecture/execution-boundary.md`).

## 1. Add a policy decision to the logic core

1. Extend the vocabulary in `crates/logic/types.rs` — a new `Event` variant
   (what the core is told) and/or a new `Effect` variant versioned with
   `op: OpId` (what the core asks for). `Event`/`Effect` are the only I/O of
   the core (`crates/logic/types.rs:3-8, 737-740`).
2. Handle the event inside the `State` method that owns that policy area and
   wire it in the `on_event` dispatcher (`crates/logic/lib.rs:5215+`). If the
   event carries time, give it `now_ms`/`now_mono_ms` stamps so `on_event`'s
   monotonic `max` fold applies (`crates/logic/lib.rs:5215-5223`).
3. Execute the effect in the Actor: add a match arm to
   `Actor::execute` (`crates/celld/actor.rs:2824+`). The established shape is
   to push a future onto `StepOutput` that performs the I/O and returns a
   `CompletedEffect::plain(Event::XxxCompleted { op, .. })` — a stale `op`
   in the completion is then ignored by the core by contract
   (`crates/celld/actor.rs:2829-2845`).
4. If the change touches a lifecycle invariant, extend `State::validate`;
   the executor asserts it after every event whenever `validate_invariants`
   is on (debug builds and simulation; too costly for release traffic)
   (`crates/celld/actor.rs:2794-2796`).

Validation: the conformance world/simulation corpora mount through
`include!(env!(...))` gates (`crates/celld/lib.rs:299-435`), so a policy
change is exercised by the seeded simulation harness; a plain `cargo test`
without the corpus env paths only compiles the gates. See
`openwiki/testing/testing-strategy.md`.

## 2. Add or change a `CELLD_*` environment variable

- Parse it through `crates/celld/env_vars.rs` only: `flag`, `positive`,
  `positive_or`, `parse_optional` (`crates/celld/env_vars.rs:115-180`). The
  contract is *"An unset variable selects its caller's documented default. A
  supplied variable must contain a valid value, so a typo cannot silently
  change the configuration of a running node"* — a Boolean accepts only `0`
  or `1`, and startup exits on invalid values (`crates/celld/env_vars.rs:3-8`,
  `docs/README.md:706-708`).
- If any consumer caches the value or reads it from a synchronous callback
  (so it cannot return an error at the point of use), add the name to
  `env_vars::validate()`'s startup pass, which makes later reads infallible
  without inventing defaults for malformed values
  (`crates/celld/env_vars.rs:10-50`).
- Build policy configuration at the edge, not in the core: e.g. the pressure
  config and ownership-on-evict policy come from `machine.rs` helpers called
  by the Actor (`crates/celld/actor.rs:6-10`), mirroring `logic::pressure`'s
  rule that "the env read that builds the config stays at the edge"
  (`crates/logic/pressure.rs:3-6`).
- Document the variable in the `docs/README.md` environment table.

Validation: the strict parsers are shared, so unit tests of `env_vars` plus
one startup run with the variable set to a bad value (expect exit) cover the
contract.

## 3. Extend the JS API surface (Workers compatibility)

- The per-isolate surface is assembled by `crates/celld/js/bootstrap.rs`:
  fixed prelude/harness scripts are compiled once per process and cached,
  while `env` bindings, the routing table, and compatibility flags differ per
  worker and are built every time (`crates/celld/js/bootstrap.rs:3-8`).
  Ops the JS layer calls back into live in `js.rs` and `js/` child modules
  (`storage_ops.rs`, `r2_ops.rs`, `websocket.rs`, `crypto.rs`, `modules.rs`).
- Remember the domain rule: `js.rs` is the raw V8 arm *outside* the Actor
  execution domain; Actor-reachable wake and WebSocket state is injected
  through `HostServices` rather than reached directly
  (`crates/celld/js.rs:2-5`, `crates/celld/host_services.rs:3-9`).
- If the surface depends on a deployment feature, gate it through the
  manifest feature flags in `crates/celld/protocol.rs` (e.g.
  `FEATURE_KV_V1`, `FEATURE_D1_V1`) (`crates/celld/protocol.rs:54-101`).

Validation: the compatibility promise is checked differentially against
workerd on identical program bytes, and the corpus only grows — a new API
surface needs fixtures that give equal output on both engines
(`docs/testing.md:39-56`). A quick manual loop is `celld dev` with one of
the `examples/` projects (the `counter` example is the standard smoke).

## 4. Change a bucket-resident object layout

`protocol.rs` is the seam: *"Durable types on the bucket contract between
deployment tools and celld. These objects are the interface; nothing else is
exchanged"* (`crates/celld/protocol.rs:1-3`). Objects include the deployment
manifest (`protocol.rs:15`), the `deploy/current.json` fleet pointer
(`protocol.rs:401`, written by `crates/celld/deploy.rs:615-619`, read via
`fleet::CURRENT_POINTER_KEY`, `crates/celld/fleet.rs:628`), the fleet secret
`fleet/peer-auth.json` (`crates/celld/peer_auth.rs:20`), node leases, and
ownership records.

- Layout changes must be safe while old readers and new writers coexist, or
  the release must demand a full stop of every node before switching — the
  docs record exactly which historical upgrades were forced stop-the-world
  and why (`docs/README.md:514-544`).
- A KV-value layout note from v0.4.0: values moved under the ownership epoch
  with an epoch-qualified row reference, and a mixed fleet could make a
  committed value unavailable — the pattern to check against
  (`docs/README.md:535-544`).
- New fleets can share a bucket only through the key prefix
  (`s3://bucket/PREFIX`), so any new key must be built from the same
  prefix-aware path (`README.md:203-208`); `ltx_repl` deliberately builds its
  own clients that carry the prefix because two fleets sharing one bucket
  would otherwise replicate over each other
  (`crates/celld/ltx_repl.rs:3-13`).

Validation: exercise against a real store — `celld diagnose` sends four
conditional writes to the target bucket (`docs/guarantees.md:59-62`) — and
keep restore paths byte-decidable: an LTX takeover reads retained bundles
under the newest safe epoch (`openwiki/concepts/durability-and-replication.md`).

## 5. Bump the peer protocol version

- The single constant is `peer_auth::PROTOCOL_VERSION` (plus its text form),
  carried on ownership/handoff answers and compared on every versioned peer
  request (`crates/celld/actor.rs:2816-2822`,
  `crates/celld/main.rs:1007, 1250`), and negotiated at tunnel establishment
  (`crates/celld/main/peer_tunnel.rs:339`). The tunnel itself is a named h1
  upgrade (`celld-tunnel`) carrying plain HTTP with `x-cells-*` control
  headers (`crates/celld/main/peer_tunnel.rs:3-14, 40`).
- The establishment step is the intended negotiation point: "The tunnel
  establishment carries the version, so a later protocol change can negotiate
  instead of refuse" (`docs/README.md:535-544`). Today refusal is what ships:
  v0.4.0 refuses a different version outright, which is why that upgrade is
  not a rolling update (`docs/README.md:535-544`).
- If the change alters what a stale body could mean, re-check the replay and
  clock-window predicates in `logic/peer.rs` — they are SECURITY fences
  (`crates/logic/peer.rs:3-8`).

Validation: `celld diagnose` reports peers whose protocol versions do not
agree (`docs/README.md:553-568`); the mixed-version handshake is exactly the
`PROTOCOL_VERSION` equality checks above.

## 6. Touch the object-store dialect

`bucket.rs` is the engine's single object-store client, and callers never see
which conditional-write dialect is active: S3/Azure use etag `If-Match` /
`If-None-Match`; GCS uses `x-goog-if-generation-match` because Cloud Storage
does not apply `If-Match` to a PUT (`crates/celld/bucket.rs:3-17`). Preserve
the error contract relied on by self-fencing: `put_cas` answers `Ok(None)`
*only* for a clean 412/409 rejection; everything else is ambiguous (the write
may have committed) and surfaces as `Err`; a response without a CAS token is
an error, never a trusted empty token (`crates/celld/bucket.rs:13-17`).

Validation: run the storage test against the store (`celld diagnose`'s four
conditional writes, `docs/guarantees.md:59-62`) and qualify a store only by
updating the qualified list in `docs/guarantees.md` with the properties it
demonstrates (`docs/guarantees.md:27-44`).

## Change hygiene

- Respect the boundary lints: never call raw `tokio::spawn`/time/`std::fs`
  inside the execution domain; route through `asyncrt`, or place the code in
  a module that documents itself as outside the domain
  (`clippy.toml:1-90`, `crates/celld/Cargo.toml:20-21`).
- Keep the fork of truth small: every direct dependency is versioned once in
  `[workspace.dependencies]` (`Cargo.toml:33-35`).
- Commit messages in this project carry rationale the way the code comments
  do — when a pin, a profile, or a fence looks odd, the explanation belongs
  next to it, not only in the PR.

part.text: Submitting claims for the change-guides page.

claims.statement: A new core policy is added by extending the Event/Effect vocabulary in types.rs and dispatching in on_event; time-bearing events must carry now_ms/now_mono_ms stamps so the core clock advances only via the monotonic max fold.

Effects are executed by adding an arm to Actor::execute, which pushes a future onto StepOutput that performs the I/O and replies with a CompletedEffect carrying an Event versioned by the effect's OpId; the core ignores completions whose op is obsolete.

Lifecycle invariant changes are guarded by State::validate, which the executor re-checks after every event when validate_invariants is enabled (debug builds and simulation), because the full cell-table scan is too expensive for release traffic.

CELLD_* variables are parsed only through env_vars helpers with the strict contract: unset selects the documented default, a supplied value must be valid (Booleans accept only 0/1), and celld exits at startup on invalid values rather than defaulting a typo.
Variables whose consumers cache the value or read it synchronously must be added to env_vars::validate's startup pass, making those reads infallible without granting malformed values a default.

Environment-derived policy configuration is built at the edge (machine.rs helpers called by the Actor), never inside celld-logic, mirroring logic::pressure's rule that the env read and the measurement stay outside the pure classifier.

The JS API surface is assembled in js/bootstrap.rs: the prelude and harness compile once per process and are cached, while per-worker bindings (env, routing table, compatibility flags) are built for each isolate.
Every new Workers/DO API surface is validated by differential fixtures run on identical program bytes against workerd and celld, and the conformance corpus only grows.

Bucket-resident objects are the durable contract between deployment tools and celld and are typed in protocol.rs, including the deploy/current.json fleet pointer written by celld deploy and read through fleet::CURRENT_POINTER_KEY.

A bucket key prefix lets two fleets share one bucket, so new keys must be prefix-aware; ltx_repl deliberately builds its own object-store clients that carry the prefix because two fleets replicating over each other is the failure mode.

bucket.rs exposes one object-store client whose CAS token is an opaque read-answered, write-consumed string, hiding the per-provider dialect: S3 and Azure speak etag If-Match/If-None-Match, GCS speaks x-goog-if-generation-match because it ignores If-Match on PUT.

put_cas answers Ok(None) only for a clean 412/409 conditional rejection; every other failure is ambiguous (possibly committed) and surfaces as Err, and a response without a CAS token is an error — this contract is what the self-fence relies on.
The peer protocol version is the single peer_auth::PROTOCOL_VERSION constant, compared on versioned peer requests, attached to handoff adoption answers, and carried on tunnel establishment.

Protocol bumps currently refuse mixed versions (v0.3.0 to v0.4.0 must not be a rolling update because the peer protocol refuses a different version), and the tunnel establishment is documented as the intended negotiation point for future version changes.
Storage-contract changes are validated with the storage test: celld diagnose sends four conditional writes to the target bucket and reports which required property the store fails.

input.content:
---
type: concept
title: "Cell-Backed Services: KV, D1, Queues, Alarms, Cron, Workflows"
description: "How celld implements Cloudflare KV, D1, Queues, cron triggers, and Workflows as reserved-class cells with their own SQLite state in the durable replication path, plus the alarm/wake machinery and the signed operator route that reaches them."
tags: [kv, d1, queues, alarms, cron, workflows, reserved-classes]
---

## The pattern: every product is a cell

celld does not build separate stores for KV, D1, Queues, or cron. Each is
one or more **reserved-class** Durable Objects — cells whose class names
start with `__` (or `.cron`) — holding real data in the same replicated
SQLite machinery as application objects, so the fleet bucket listing marks
them `"reserved": true` (`docs/README.md:596-605`). The policy math lives in
`celld-logic` (`kv.rs`, `queue.rs`, `cron.rs`, `alarm.rs`, `wake.rs`), the
SQL and dispatch live in the cells, and the operators reach them through
signed runtime routes.

| Service | Class | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D1 database | `__D1Database` | fleet-wide, shared across scripts on purpose (`crates/celld/deploy.rs:59-64, 108-116`) |
| KV namespace | `__KvNamespace` | fleet-wide: two scripts naming one namespace reach one set of cells (`crates/logic/kv.rs:27-35`) |
| Queue broker | `__Queue` | fleet-wide (`crates/logic/queue.rs:18-19`) |
| Workflows | `__Workflow.<script>` | script-scoped (`crates/celld/deploy.rs:66-68, 83-104`) |
| Cron schedule | `.cron` | one cell per script (`crates/logic/cron.rs:33, 41`) |

These runtime-supplied classes are *refused* as user class names in
`durable_objects` or `migrations` config, because the harness registers them
in every isolate and a user binding would silently reach engine state
(`crates/celld/deploy.rs:59-63, 66-68`). The workflow class carries the
script name with a `.` separator for three stated reasons — JS class names
cannot contain `.` (no user collision), it is not `:` (the scope split
character), and it is inside `cell::valid_cell_scope`'s security-fence
charset (`crates/celld/deploy.rs:83-104`). D1 deliberately stays unscoped:
its namespace is fleet-wide so a database outlives the name of any Worker
that binds it (`crates/celld/deploy.rs:90-97, 106-116`).

Reserved classes also decide an access boundary: `is_reserved_class` gates
which classes *refuse an unauthenticated operator route*, and `.cron` is
named beside that predicate rather than added to it, so the cron cell stays
reachable (`crates/celld/generation.rs:347-357`).

## KV

A KV namespace is a cell; `celld_logic::kv` keeps only what decides an
address or publishes a bound — the bounds themselves, the shard function,
the cell name, and the large-value reference (`crates/logic/kv.rs:3-24`).
Upstream limits are refused, not truncated: 512-byte keys, 25 MiB values,
1 KiB metadata, a 60-second minimum expiry TTL (`crates/logic/kv.rs:37-59`).
Values up to **1 MiB** live inline in the namespace cell's SQLite; above
that the bytes go to the fleet bucket and the row names them, because a
cell's writes replicate as LTX and an inline value is paid for twice — the
split was set by an A/B finding the inline path wins at 1 MiB and the bucket
path at 2 MiB (`crates/logic/kv.rs:40-52`). Since v0.4.0 a new large value
is stored under its ownership epoch with an epoch-qualified row reference,
which is why a v0.3.x node cannot read it and the upgrade is stop-the-world
(`docs/README.md:535-544`). The key/value bound checks live once in the
JS harness, fed as data (`__cell.kvLimits`) by the same module — the Rust
copies became "tested by the DST, run by nobody" and were deleted
(`crates/logic/kv.rs:9-18`).

## Queues

A queue is one reserved cell; `celld_logic::queue` owns "the stable address,
the public bounds, the alarm deadline, concurrency admission, retry timing,
lease-generation advancement, settlement fencing, purge classification, and
deploy-time configuration validation" (`crates/logic/queue.rs:3-9`). The
public bounds mirror Cloudflare (128 000-byte messages, 100-per-batch, up to
100 retries, 250 max concurrency), with 4-day retention fixed for celld v1
because Wrangler has no key for it (`crates/logic/queue.rs:21-38`). The
queue name is the cell name unchanged — the identity function is
deliberate, so a project addresses the same queue as Cloudflare, and both
binding and operator CLI call the one function before the runtime applies
the namespace HMAC (`crates/logic/queue.rs:41-49`).

Delivery safety rests on the **lease generation**: it travels inside
`PlannedLease`, and the module never returns a bare sequence number for a
deliverable row, so a late settlement from an expired lease cannot
acknowledge a newer delivery (`crates/logic/queue.rs:11-16`). Under a hot
queue the broker shares the cell-admission rule: at `CELLD_MAX_CELL_REQUESTS`
(default 64) concurrent events celld answers 503 with `X-Celld-Overload:
cell` and a `cell_overload_refused` log event (`docs/README.md:638-655`).
Operators run `celld queue info|pause|resume` through the signed route below
(`README.md:250-257`).

## D1

Every D1 database is a `__D1Database` cell, registered by the harness in
each isolate (`crates/celld/deploy.rs:59-64, 1104-1107`). Because it is one
cell, D1 SQL rides the ordinary durability path — the same output gate that
holds a response until the write's LTX is proven durable
(`openwiki/concepts/durability-and-replication.md`); the docs note D1 even
restored per-cell concurrency by deleting a thread that had accidentally
forbidden it (`crates/logic/gate.rs:5-8`). `celld d1` (SQL, `migrations
apply`) finds a node through the bucket's node leases, and that node routes
the work to the node that owns the database cell (`README.md:236-240`).

## Alarms, wake entries, and cron

An alarm is a row in the cell's own SQLite; its retry policy is a pure
function of the row's retry counters — exponential backoff with a bounded
count of limit-counting failures before abandonment — and storage is the
executor (`crates/logic/alarm.rs:3-8`). A cell's alarm survives eviction
because committed alarm state is **mirrored to the bucket** as
`wake/<YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM>/<cell>` entries: the sweep only evicts an
alarm-bearing cell behind a durable entry, a per-node boot scan plus heap
re-activates due cells, and a per-fleet advisory waker revives orphans whose
owner died. The simulation-verified invariants: arm durable ⟹ entry exists
within one sweep tick; only completed activation or a durable consume
deletes an entry; and a successful response is never sent until a durable
wake entry covers an alarm set before the response boundary
(`crates/celld/wake.rs:3-15`, `docs/README.md:67-70`).

Cron triggers reuse exactly this machinery: a `triggers.crons` entry becomes
one reserved cell per script (`.cron`), and "ownership CAS on this one name
is what makes a cron fire once per fleet" — each occurrence arms the cell's
alarm (`crates/logic/cron.rs:3-12, 35-39`). The expression dialect is
Cloudflare's (the `saffron` parser), not POSIX, because the two disagree on
day numbering (`crates/logic/cron.rs:16-20, 86-90`).

## Workflows

Workflow instances run as script-scoped `__Workflow.<script>` cells
(`crates/celld/deploy.rs:83-104`); the feature is negotiated through the
deployment manifest flag `FEATURE_WORKFLOWS_V1`
(`crates/celld/protocol.rs:87`), and the workflow bindings are injected at
isolate bootstrap (`crates/celld/js/bootstrap.rs:310-334`). Step returns
share the 1 MiB inline cap that motivated the KV split
(`crates/logic/kv.rs:52`).

## Reaching reserved cells from the CLI

`operator_cell.rs` is the shared machinery behind `celld d1`, `celld kv`,
and `celld queue`: find a live node through the bucket leases, sign the
request with the fleet secret, and post to `/runtime/<scope>`, which
forwards to the cell's owner. The alternatives are explicitly rejected in
the code comments — writing the object in the bucket directly would write
*behind the fence* (the owner's next flush overwrites it), and naming one
node fails because the internal listener's port is ephemeral by default
(`crates/celld/operator_cell.rs:3-14`). That refusal is why reserved
classes reject unauthenticated operator routes (`crates/celld/generation.rs:351-355`).

## See also

- `openwiki/architecture/logic-decision-core.md` — the policy modules.
- `openwiki/concepts/durability-and-replication.md` — what "durable" means
  for these cells' SQL.
- `openwiki/operations/fleet-operations.md` — the operator commands and
  limits.

A saturated Queue broker or Durable Object refuses admission with HTTP 503, Retry-After: 1, X-Celld-Overload: cell, and a cell_overload_refused log event, under the shared per-cell concurrent-event limit (default 64).

Alarm retry policy is a pure function of the alarm row's retry counters — exponential backoff with a bounded number of limit-counting failures before abandonment — persisted by the cell's own SQLite storage.

celld does not send a successful response until a durable wake entry covers an alarm set before the response boundary, and a later waitUntil alarm cannot delay another event's response.

A triggers.crons entry becomes one reserved .cron cell per script whose alarm is armed at the next occurrence, ownership CAS on that single name is what makes a cron fire once per fleet, and the expression dialect is Cloudflare's saffron parser rather than POSIX cron.

The test writes and deletes one small object under `probe/`. A process
that stops mid-test can leave the object behind; it is small, and celld
never reads it. celld reserves `probe/` together with `cells/`,
`nodes/`, `node-cells/`, `fleet/`, `deploy/`, `deploy-blobs/`, `wake/`,
and `telemetry/`, and it deletes objects under some of them, so an
application must not write under any of these prefixes.

celld does not require a ranged read today, so a store that ignores the
`Range` header can still run a fleet.

## The supervisor

You must run celld under a supervisor that restarts the process, such
as systemd, Docker with a restart policy, or Kubernetes. A node fences
itself when it loses its lease (the mechanism is below), and a fenced
process exits; without a restart, the fleet loses that capacity until
an operator intervenes.

The supervisor must restart without an attempt limit, and it must wait
at least one lease lifetime between attempts. A node that cannot
acquire a lease at startup retries and does not exit, so a repeated
fence needs a node that acquires a lease and then loses it, and the
wait keeps that cycle slow enough to observe.

## The mechanism

The short version: the ownership records use conditional writes, so two
nodes cannot acquire one cell. The replicated data carries its fencing
epoch in the object key, so a node that lost ownership writes only into
a superseded prefix. And before celld acknowledges a write, it proves
the write durable and confirms that it still owns the cell.

### The ownership record

Each cell has one ownership record in the bucket. The record names the
owner node's session and carries a fencing epoch. A node acquires a
cell with a conditional write — a create when no record exists, a
compare-and-swap on the previous record when one does — and the bucket
accepts one such write, so two nodes cannot acquire the same cell.

Every activation advances the epoch, a takeover and a local wake alike.
Each owner therefore replicates under a fresh epoch, and an epoch never
has two writers.

### The epoch prefix

The replicator copies each cell's SQLite data to the bucket under
`cells/<cell>/ltx/e<epoch>/`, with plain unconditional PUTs. The epoch
in the key is the fence: a node that lost ownership can keep writing,
but its writes land in a superseded prefix, and a restore selects the
current lineage. (The tiering path can first combine segments from many
cells into a node bundle, and it drains each segment into its per-cell
prefix later.)

The prefix protects the new owner's data from stale writes. The next
two sections protect the durability promise.

### The acknowledgement rule (RPO=0)

A gate holds each write response until a durability proof covers the
write. After a bucket proof, celld reads the ownership record once and
acknowledges only if the record still names this node at this epoch. A
partitioned node can commit locally and replicate into its superseded
prefix, but the ownership read then shows the new owner, so celld does
not acknowledge the write. The check reads the record instead of
comparing a clock, so a paused process or a skewed clock cannot pass
it.

A fleet proof does not require this read. The owner sends each write to
one or two other nodes, which hold a copy of its recent writes; those
nodes are its followers, and the set of them is the ensemble. Every
follower must fsync the write, and a takeover seals the prior node-log
session before it restores, so the stale owner cannot complete another
fleet proof.

### The ensemble needs two nodes

A node picks its followers from the other nodes in the fleet, so it never
counts itself. One follower is enough, therefore a fleet needs two
running celld nodes before any node can complete a fleet proof.
`CELLD_DURABILITY=fleet` is the default, so a fleet of one node requests the
fleet posture and does not get it.

A node recruits up to two followers, so a fleet of three or more nodes holds
three copies of an acknowledged write. The ensemble keeps acknowledging while
one follower remains, therefore a fleet does not fall back to the bucket each
time it loses a follower.

A node without an ensemble stays correct. It acknowledges each write on a
bucket proof instead, so celld still does not acknowledge a write before a
durability proof covers it. The cost is latency: the write waits for the object
store, and an object store round trip is much slower than a follower fsync.

### The takeover recovery gate

The default fleet mode can acknowledge a write once the node-log
ensemble stores it; the bucket upload can complete later. Each process
session therefore creates a conditional node-log record before its
first fleet-durable acknowledgement.

A cold activation checks the prior owner's log records before it reads
the bucket. An absent record proves that the session never acknowledged
past the bucket, and a sealed record proves that recovery completed. An
open or recovering record makes the activation run recovery: it fences
the record with a compare-and-swap, seals the reachable followers,
uploads their retained segments and bundles into the per-cell prefixes,
and then marks the record sealed. The activation cannot restore until
this sequence completes.

### Full-prefix restore

A restore selects the newest epoch prefix that contains LTX data, and
it reads the full contiguous chain from transaction zero. celld no
longer writes an epoch seal object, and a legacy `e<epoch>.seal.json`
object does not limit the chain.

A fenced node can append an unacknowledged tail to an older prefix, and
a later restore can expose that tail. This does not violate the
contract, because a failed or absent acknowledgement does not prove
that the write is absent. The rule reads the full chain because a
node-log recovery or a bundle drain can add an acknowledged tail after
an earlier restore; a restore that stopped at the earlier cut would
hide that tail and lose acknowledged data.

### Self-fencing

Each node holds a lease in the bucket. The lease carries an expiry, and
the node renews it after one third of the lifetime (`CELLD_TTL_MS`,
default 10000 ms). A renewal that does not reach the bucket does not
fence the node, because the node retries while the published expiry has
not passed.

A node that cannot reach the bucket cannot renew and cannot replicate,
so it must not own cells. When its published expiry passes, it fences
itself: it stops each active cell, and it fails every request that it
has not completed. A node whose lease record another writer replaced or
removed fences at once, because that record proves the authority moved.

The fence writes nothing to the bucket. Each peer already reads the
lease as dead or replaced, so a peer can acquire the cells through the
ownership records. And a request is safe even before the fence runs,
because celld compares the current time against the published expiry
each time it routes a request.

A fenced node logs a line that starts with `SELF-FENCE:` and stops with
the exit code 3. celld reports other internal failures with the same
prefix and code, so the line names the cause. The fenced state is
terminal: only a restart returns the node to the fleet, through the
same cold-activation path that a peer failure uses.

The failure of a node is a normal input, not a recovery procedure; the
[testing page](testing.md) shows the kill tests that exercise this
path.

input.content:
---
type: concept
title: "Cells, Ownership, and Fencing"
description: "How celld keeps exactly one node serving each cell without consensus: bucket ownership records with conditional writes, epochs as the data-path fence, node leases and lease-based request admission, dead-node takeover with the node-log recovery gate, and terminal self-fencing."
tags: [ownership, fencing, epochs, node-lease, takeover, self-fence]
---

## Two fences, one guarantee

celld's safety promise — one writer per cell at a time — rests on two
independent mechanisms, and the split is deliberate:

- **Control path: the ownership record.** Each cell has one bucket record
  naming the owner's node session and carrying a fencing epoch. Acquisition
  is a conditional write — a create-if-absent, or a compare-and-swap on the
  previous record — so the bucket itself decides the winner: "two nodes
  cannot acquire the same cell" (`docs/guarantees.md:100-108`). The
  decisions (claim, release, takeover) are `celld-logic` transitions;
  `ownership_store.rs` "deliberately contains serialization, wall-clock
  sampling, SDK configuration and error classification only"
  (`crates/celld/ownership_store.rs:3-6`).
- **Data path: the epoch prefix.** Committed SQLite data replicates to
  `cells/<cell>/ltx/e<epoch>/` with plain unconditional PUTs — "The epoch
  in the key is the fence: a node that lost ownership can keep writing, but
  its writes land in a superseded prefix, and a restore selects the current
  lineage" (`docs/guarantees.md:110-116`, `crates/celld/replication.rs:3-7`).
  Every activation advances the epoch — takeover and local wake alike
  (`docs/guarantees.md:106-108`); in the core the successor epoch is literally
  `record.epoch + 1` on claim (`crates/logic/lib.rs:3228, 3244, 3539`), and
  the executor's own comment states "epoch-in-prefix is the data-path fence:
  a stale owner writes a dead prefix" (`crates/celld/replication.rs:6-7`).

Because the two fences are independent, the argument for acknowledged writes
does not need clocks: "The check reads the record instead of comparing a
clock, so a paused process or a skewed clock cannot pass it"
(`docs/guarantees.md:126-128`).

## Lifecycle: resident, hibernated, dormant, inactive

The doc set and the `Phase` machine agree (`docs/README.md:22-33`,
`crates/logic/lib.rs:105-170`): a **resident** cell is in memory (active
while working, idle while waiting); celld removes an idle cell from memory;
a cell that keeps its hibernatable WebSocket clients and stays on its node
is **hibernated** — the `Phase::Dormant { epoch }` entry, "Out of memory,
still owned here. Hibernated when sockets survived"
(`crates/logic/lib.rs:166-168`); a cell no node holds is **inactive**, "only
an object in the bucket" (`docs/README.md:28-29`). The vocabulary trap is
documented in the code: celld "evicts" a cell *out of memory* (→ `Dormant`)
and *sheds* by publishing it unowned, while Cloudflare's "evict" means
off-host (`crates/logic/lib.rs:106-110`).

Memory-pressure shedding uses exactly that path: under pressure celld
durably replicates and fences the least-recently-used idle cells, "publishes
them as unowned without resetting their epochs," and refuses to reacquire
new unowned cells until pressure passes; cells with active work or a live
host WebSocket are never shed (`README.md:288-295`).

## Node leases: fleet membership without membership

A **fleet** is simply the nodes sharing one bucket; discovery and authority
both come from the bucket (`docs/README.md:38-45`). Each node holds a node
lease record with a published expiry (`NodeLeaseSpec.ttl_ms`, default
10 000 ms from `CELLD_TTL_MS`; `crates/celld/actor.rs:2091`,
`crates/celld/machine.rs:54`). The core renews after *one third* of the
lifetime (`spec.ttl_ms / 3`, `crates/logic/lib.rs:1849, 1934, 1973`), and a
renewal that fails to reach the bucket does not fence the node while the
published expiry is still future — it retries (`docs/guarantees.md:176-180`).

Requests check authority before routing, not after: peers "treat a lease as
dead the instant `now_ms` reaches `expires_ms`"
(`crates/logic/lib.rs:714-717`), and routing "compares the current time
against the published expiry each time it routes a request," so a request is
safe even before a partitioned node notices its own fence
(`docs/guarantees.md:194-196`). The expiry is anchored to the monotonic
instant it was computed from, not the write completion
(`crates/logic/lib.rs:1914-1942`).

## Takeover: read the old owner's log first

The cold-start walk is the `Phase` machine above
(`Inactive → ReadingOwner → …Acquiring → Restoring → Starting → Publishing`;
`crates/logic/lib.rs:105-170`). Before a takeover restores from the bucket,
the new owner runs the **recovery gate**: each process session creates a
conditional node-log record before its first fleet-durable ack, so an
*absent* record proves the dead session never acknowledged past the bucket
and a *sealed* record proves recovery completed; an open or recovering
record forces recovery first — fence the record, seal reachable followers,
upload their retained segments into the per-cell prefixes, mark sealed —
and "the activation cannot restore until this sequence completes"
(`docs/guarantees.md:148-160`). In the state machine this is
`Phase::RecoveringOwnerLog`, "the takeover interlock (lease-fold): the dead
owner's folded log state was not sealed, so the executor is recovering its
sessions before this cell may claim" (`crates/logic/lib.rs:121-126`).

Restore itself reads the full chain: it selects the newest epoch prefix
containing LTX data and reads from transaction zero, because a node-log
recovery or bundle drain can add an acknowledged tail *after* an earlier
cut — "a restore that stopped at the earlier cut would hide that tail and
lose acknowledged data" (`docs/guarantees.md:162-172`).

## Self-fencing is terminal

A node that cannot reach the bucket cannot renew and cannot replicate, so
"it must not own cells": once its published expiry passes, it fences itself,
stops every active cell, and fails every incomplete request
(`docs/guarantees.md:174-186`). The executor path is `Actor`'s fence flow:
`fence_node` sets the core to fenced, drains the output gate to
`Err(NodeFenced)` atomically with the authority loss, and emits
`Effect::Halt { code: 3, reason: HaltReason::NodeLeaseExpired }`
(`crates/logic/lib.rs:5076-5100, 2810-2815`); the actor logs
`"SELF-FENCE: node lease not renewed within TTL — halting"` and the process
exits with code 3 (`crates/celld/actor.rs:3738`). The fence deliberately
writes *nothing* to the bucket — peers already read the lease as dead — and
the state is terminal: only a restart returns the node to the fleet, through
the same cold-activation path a peer failure uses (`docs/guarantees.md:188-196`).

Because fencing only *exits*, the operator contract is a supervisor:
restart without an attempt limit, waiting at least one lease lifetime
between attempts, since "a node that cannot acquire a lease at startup
retries and does not exit" (`docs/guarantees.md:85-96`).

## Graceful release is a different path

Planned shutdown does not wait for expiry: the draining node hands cells off
in batches — prove durable, publish a final L9 snapshot where possible,
release the ownership record, and ask a compatible peer to adopt it (the
peer acknowledges after the ownership update and keeps the cell dormant, so
handoff never restores an unused runtime) (`docs/README.md:441-455`).
Concurrent donors serialize through the advisory fleet drain token
(`crates/celld/drain_token.rs:3-9`, `crates/logic/drain.rs:3-9`), and the
full procedure is `openwiki/operations/fleet-operations.md`.

## See also

- `openwiki/integrations/object-storage.md` — the conditional-write
  dialects the records depend on.
- `openwiki/concepts/durability-and-replication.md` — the ack rule the
  fences protect.
- `openwiki/concepts/http-routing-and-peer-tunnel.md` — reading a lease to
  route a request.

claims.statement: Cell exclusivity on the control path is a single bucket ownership record per cell acquired by conditional write (create-if-absent or compare-and-swap on the previous record), with ownership decisions held in celld-logic while ownership_store.rs performs only serialization, clock sampling, SDK configuration, and error classification.

Every activation advances the fencing epoch (successor epoch = record.epoch + 1 in the core), and replicated data is written under cells/<scope>/ltx/e<epoch>/ with plain unconditional PUTs, so a stale owner's late writes land only in a superseded, dead prefix.
The durability acknowledgement check re-reads the ownership record instead of comparing clocks, so a paused process or skewed clock cannot pass it after ownership moved.

The cell lifecycle distinguishes resident (active/idle), hibernated (out of memory as Phase::Dormant while keeping hibernatable WebSockets on the same node), and inactive (bucket-only, owned by nobody), and the code documents that celld 'evicts' out of memory while Cloudflare's evict means off-host.

Memory-pressure shedding durably replicates and fences least-recently-used idle cells, publishes them unowned without resetting their epochs, refuses reacquisition of new unowned cells while shedding, and never sheds a cell with active work or a live host WebSocket.

Fleet membership needs no protocol: nodes sharing one bucket discover each other through node lease records, and each node holds its lease with a published expiry governed by CELLD_TTL_MS (default 10000 ms).

The core renews the node lease at one third of its lifetime, and a renewal that fails to reach the bucket does not fence the node while the published expiry remains future because the node keeps retrying.
Request routing treats a lease as dead the instant now_ms reaches the published expiry, so forwarded requests are safe against a partitioned owner even before that owner's own fence runs.

Before a takeover restores, the new owner checks the dead owner's node-log record: absent proves the session never acknowledged past the bucket, sealed proves recovery completed, and an open or recovering record forces the Phase::RecoveringOwnerLog lease-fold recovery (fence the record, seal followers, upload retained segments) before any restore.

Restore reads the full contiguous LTX chain from transaction zero in the newest epoch prefix containing data, because node-log recovery or bundle drains can append an acknowledged tail after an earlier restore point.

Self-fencing is terminal: when the published lease expiry passes (or the record is replaced/removed), the core fences, emits Effect::Halt with code 3 and HaltReason::NodeLeaseExpired, the actor logs 'SELF-FENCE: node lease not renewed within TTL', and only a restart rejoins the fleet.
The fence writes nothing to the bucket — peers already read the lease as dead or replaced — and gated outputs fail rather than acknowledge, making the fence and the failed write atomic.

Operators must run celld under an unlimited-attempt restart supervisor waiting at least one lease lifetime between attempts, because a fenced process exits while a node that merely cannot acquire a lease at startup retries without exiting.

Planned shutdown releases ownership in paced batches with durable proofs and final snapshots plus successor acknowledgements, while concurrent donors serialize on the advisory bucket drain token and a donor that cannot claim it within its bound proceeds anyway.

input.content:
---
type: concept
title: "Durability, Replication, and the Output Gate"
description: "The RPO=0 write path: WAL-to-LTX capture per cell, the output gate holding every revealing response until a durability proof, bucket tiering as the permanent path, the fleet node-log tier with a write-all/ack-all ensemble, hedging, gray-follower eviction, and recovery."
tags: [durability, rpo-zero, ltx, node-log, output-gate, replication]
---

## The promise, and the two proof routes

celld answers a write only after the write survives a failure — RPO=0 —
and the proof comes from one of two places (`docs/guarantees.md:98-145`):

- **Bucket proof** (always available, always true): the cell's committed
  transaction data is uploaded to the object store under the live epoch
  prefix, and the owner then re-reads the ownership record and acknowledges
  only if it still names this node at this epoch. A partitioned node can
  replicate into its superseded prefix, but the ownership read shows the new
  owner and the write is not acknowledged
  (`docs/guarantees.md:130-141`).
- **Fleet proof** (default posture, `CELLD_DURABILITY=fleet`): the owner
  streams the same data to one or two follower nodes, which fsync it; the
  write is durable once every ensemble member holds it — write-all, ack-all
  — or once the bucket upload finishes first, whichever wins
  (`crates/celld/node_log.rs:3-12`). A follower fsync beats a storage round
  trip: one lab measured ~600 ms bucket proof vs ~25 ms fleet proof, and a
  bucket that races every fleet proof means a slow follower cannot make a
  write slower than a bucket proof (`docs/testing.md:171-177`).

The fleet proof needs *two running nodes*: a node picks followers only among
*other* nodes, so a fleet of one requests the posture and never gets it, and
falls back to bucket-proof acks (`docs/guarantees.md:151-168`). A node
recruits up to two followers, so three or more nodes hold three copies of an
acknowledged write and acks continue while one follower remains
(`docs/guarantees.md:159-162`).

## The output gate: where durability becomes a response policy

The gate is one rule in the core, executed by the shell: *"Nothing that
reveals a cell's state may leave this process while that cell has a write it
cannot prove durable"* (`crates/logic/output_gate.rs:6-10`). SQL writes
commit synchronously inside the cell isolate; the response (and every other
`Channel` egress) is held in the core's barrier map, keyed by the durability
`OpId` — "an open gate makes its cell active, so the cell cannot be evicted
underneath it; a fence drains these to a failed response"
(`crates/logic/lib.rs:509-515`). When a proof (bucket confirm or ensemble
ack) resolves the barrier, the core emits `Effect::Release` and the held
output leaves (`crates/logic/output_gate.rs:12-31`). `CELLD_OUTPUT_GATE=0`
removes the wait — and accepts possible loss of an acknowledged write — by
the shell simply not routing outputs through the gate
(`crates/celld/actor.rs:1751-1756`, `docs/README.md:690`). Alarms have the
same rule: a successful response waits until a durable wake entry covers an
alarm set before the response boundary (`docs/README.md:67-70`).

## Capture: from SQLite commit to LTX

Each resident cell owns a managed `celld_ltx::Db` that captures the
committed WAL as LTX segments and uploads on demand — "no external process,
no directory-watch lag", and a just-written cell is registered the instant
it activates, so the gate can prove a fresh cell durable with no cold-start
window (`crates/celld/ltx_repl.rs:3-9`). Per-cell layout: local
`<watch>/<cell>/ltx/e<epoch>/db.sqlite` mirroring the bucket's
`cells/<cell>/ltx/e<epoch>/`, which is the data-path fence
(`crates/celld/replication.rs:3-7`). Two tuning behaviors matter for the
capture read cost: at `CELLD_LTX_TRUNCATE_PAGES` (default 128 pages ≈ 512
KiB) an ordinary cell's WAL is truncated at the next checkpoint, because a
passive checkpoint never shrinks the file and every capture re-reads the
stale tail; queue cells keep passive checkpoints because the truncate
boundary emits a full database image (`docs/README.md:695`). Background
additive L1 compaction (`CELLD_LTX_COMPACTION=1`, default) means a takeover
reads tens of objects instead of thousands (`docs/README.md:696-698`), and
node-log tiering may first pack many cells' L0 segments into bundle objects
that drain into the per-cell prefixes later
(`docs/guarantees.md:121-127`, `crates/ltx/src/bundle.rs:3-8`).

Throughput note: concurrent writes to one cell join one shared upload, so
one cell is not one round trip per write (`docs/testing.md:175-177`).

## The node-log tier in detail

`crates/celld/node_log.rs` is the executor of `crates/logic/log_tier.rs`
decisions ("The decisions are `celld_logic::log_tier`; this module is their
executor", `crates/celld/node_log.rs:11-12`). Core safety rules, each
load-bearing (`crates/logic/log_tier.rs:12-21`):

- A follower's (ensemble, epoch) view changes **only with the bucket
  record**, never on the leader's stream alone.
- A follower refuses appends at or below its persisted seal mark.
- Reconfiguration force-tiers the open fragment through the new fragment
  base before the CAS, so an empty joiner is covered entirely by the bucket.
- Recovery seals before it certifies, and certifies from a sealed member
  only.
- `log/<node>.json` is created before the node's first fleet-durable ack and
  **never deleted**, so a takeover finding no record may treat the bucket
  as complete (`crates/celld/node_log.rs:9-11`).

The record itself (`LogRecord`: epoch, ensemble, tiered offset,
`LogState ∈ {Open, Recovering, Sealed}`) is mutated only by conditional
writes, and "the executor must treat a lost CAS as anothers' turn, never
retry blindly" (`crates/logic/log_tier.rs:41-49`). The lease renewal folds
this state in: `Event::NodeLeaseCasCompleted` carries the `stamped_log_state`
the shell serialized into *that* attempt's body, because the shell stamps
from its own slot after the core chose `desired`, so the core's readback
must use the stamped value and never its pre-attempt belief
(`crates/logic/types.rs:415-425`).

**Hedging and eviction.** A slow append is hedged: after `CELLD_LOG_HEDGE_MS`
the leader sends a second copy to a follower; the default is adaptive — 4×
the slowest recent append, floored at 250 ms, always below the eviction
backstop — and appends are idempotent per sequence, so the leader uses the
first answer (`docs/README.md:694`). The gray-follower policy lives in
`crates/logic/log_evict.rs`: one slow follower stalls every ack under
write-all, so the leader evicts on suspicion when the follower's windowed
append-latency tail exceeds the bound, and the empty-join reconfiguration
makes a false positive cost exactly one flush plus one CAS
(`crates/logic/log_evict.rs:3-8`). The executor reads the policy from env
with the design-doc defaults (`crates/celld/node_log.rs:206-229`), and the
append lane arms its hedge deadline bounded by the eviction backstop rather
than the generic client timeout (`crates/celld/node_log.rs:1656-1662`).

**Bounded failure semantics (v0, deliberate):** entries travel as base64
JSON; a follower failure degrades the node to bucket-proof acks until a
periodic re-recruit CASes a fresh ensemble; recovery gathers from every
reachable *sealed* member and **requires at least one**
(`crates/celld/node_log.rs:13-16`).

## Recovery, sealing, and takeover

Each process session's `log/<node>.json` is also the takeover interlock: a
cold activation that finds an open or recovering record runs recovery —
CAS-fences the record, seals reachable followers, uploads their retained
segments and bundles into per-cell prefixes, marks sealed — before it may
restore (`docs/guarantees.md:176-184`; `Phase::RecoveringOwnerLog`,
`crates/logic/lib.rs:121-126`). A deadline-cut handoff can leave that
recovery for the replacement: one process reads and uploads the dead
session while others wait, a waiting process may replace an unresponsive
recovery after 30 seconds, and a recovery store error keeps the session
*unsealed* so a later recovery must read every retained bundle
(`docs/README.md:491-495`).

The bucket remains the tiering mechanism unchanged — "node-log recovery
re-creates exactly the objects the dead leader would have uploaded and every
per-cell restore and compaction mechanism stays byte-for-byte as it is"
(`crates/celld/node_log.rs:7-10`) — and the restore-source choice itself is
a core decision: activation restores from the *newest SAFE* source (local
eviction snapshot vs replicated bucket), because a stale local source serves
lost writes while a needless remote restore pays dozens of sequential round
trips (`crates/logic/restore.rs:3-9`).

## The seal that was removed

History worth carrying: celld once sealed a cell's durable history at
restore; model-checking showed the seal only defended the return of a never-
acknowledged write (not a promised outcome) while its permanent cut could
turn a recoverable ordering slip into permanent loss — so the seal is gone,
and a fenced node's unacknowledged tail in an older prefix is explicitly
allowed (`docs/testing.md:67-71`, `docs/guarantees.md:190-193`).

## See also

- `openwiki/integrations/ltx-replication-engine.md` — the vendored LTX/WAL
  mechanics.
- `openwiki/concepts/cells-and-ownership.md` — the ownership read that
  completes a bucket proof.
- `openwiki/architecture/logic-decision-core.md` — the barrier map and the
  single release rule.
